title: Physiological Resilience: What Is It and How Might It Be Trained?
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
findings: Resilience is built into a modified Joyner model: start-line VO2max, economy and thresholds deteriorate during prolonged exercise, often with appreciable inter-individual variability.
Data are scant, but training consistency and accumulation of relatively large training volumes over several years might promote resilience.

Regular prolonged sessions, especially including high-intensity bouts at race pace or above or a progressive intensity increase in the face of developing fatigue, might be an effective means of enhancing resilience.
Resistance training, especially heavy strength and plyometric training, appears to have positive effects on resilience.
limitations: Narrative review that itself says data are scant; recommendations are hypotheses, not tested prescriptions. The abstract gives no specific fraction or frequency for late-run intensity.
implications: Include a regular long run in every build and add some race-pace or progressive-intensity work late in selected long runs for marathon and longer goals. The specific fraction (for example the final 20-30%) is an engineering heuristic, not a value from this paper; treat as low-to-moderate-confidence.
Keep two weekly heavy strength or plyometric sessions in a durability-focused block (supported by the RCT in this corpus, [zanini-2025-strength-economy-durability-rct]).

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed match (Scand J Med Sci Sports 2025 Mar;35(3):e70032). Crossref title contains an HTML-escaped ampersand only.
